subtype: Approach: rebuild a schedule after a salary change [Revision]
passage:
Mohit: You look pleased. Raise came through?

Jatin: Yes, a decent one. First thing I did was open the loan sheet.

Mohit: You never miss a chance for a spreadsheet.

Jatin: It matters. With the old salary, the last payment was going to be three years from now. Look, with the new figure I raise the instalment a little and it moves to two years and eight months.

Mohit: Only four months.

Jatin: Four months of interest saved. And I've set a reminder every six months to check the sheet again.

Mohit: Why every six months?

Jatin: Because things change, a bonus or a new rent. If the plan doesn't change with them, it stops being a plan.

Mohit: Fair enough. Buy me chai?

Jatin: Buy your own. I'm saving.

qa.q: How often did Jatin set the reminder to check the sheet?
qa.a: Jatin set a reminder every six months to check the sheet.

qa.q: What did Jatin feel about the raise?
qa.a: Jatin was pleased, and used the raise straight away to rework the plan instead of spending it.

qa.q: What could Jatin do if the salary falls or a big bill comes, and why?
qa.a: Jatin could reopen the sheet and lower the instalment to a safe level, because the plan is meant to change with life.

qa.q: How might Mohit see Jatin's habit of opening the sheet?
qa.a: Mohit teases Jatin and finds it a bit much, but still listens and says it is fair enough.

grounding: After a raise a borrower recalculates the payoff date in a spreadsheet, slightly increases the instalment and sets a reminder to review regularly.

passage: Wednesday night. Rekha and I were sitting on the terrace when she asked me, "What if you can't pay your loan?" Not a happy question. But I tried an exercise: imagine it's the second year and I have failed to pay. Why? Maybe I lose my job. Maybe a family medical bill comes. Maybe the phone is stolen and I forget the dates. All three could happen. So I wrote what would help: a small reserve I don't touch, the bank's helpline number in my notes, and the name of the officer at my branch. It felt a bit morbid, but strangely calming. I've moved a small amount into a separate pot tonight. Imagining the failure has made it feel less likely. Vaibhav

qa.q: What three causes of failing to pay did Vaibhav imagine?
qa.a: Vaibhav imagined losing a job, a family medical bill and a stolen phone with forgotten dates.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel after writing out the failure and the fixes?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt it was a bit morbid but strangely calming, since each cause now had a small answer.

qa.q: What else could Vaibhav do to be ready, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could talk to the bank early if any of those problems really happen, because early contact keeps options open.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Vaibhav's answer to a gloomy question?
qa.a: Rekha may be surprised that Vaibhav turned a worry into a plan, and may want to do the same.

grounding: A borrower imagines defaulting in the second year, lists causes such as job loss or a medical bill, and keeps a reserve and a bank contact.

subtype: Approach: set up auto-debit with a reminder [Action]
passage:
Friday. Simran opened the bank site and linked the instalment for the education loan to auto-debit, set to leave the account the day after salary arrives. Damini, who had missed a due date last year, watched over the shoulder.

Next Thursday. A text arrived: "Balance below the set limit." Simran had added that alert too. The salary was a day late and the alert gave time to move money across before the debit.

Two months later. Simran opened the passbook. Both instalments had gone on time. "Automation only works if I still look at the balance," Simran said. Damini set up the same thing that evening.

qa.q: When was the auto-debit set to leave the account?
qa.a: The auto-debit was set for the day after salary arrives.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when the low-balance alert arrived?
qa.a: Simran was probably relieved, because the alert came in time to move money across before the debit despite the late salary.

qa.q: What could Simran do if the salary is delayed again, and why?
qa.a: Simran could keep a small buffer in the account, because a late salary should not cause a missed debit.

qa.q: How might Damini see Simran's auto-debit after the missed date last year?
qa.a: Damini probably felt encouraged, since the plan solved a problem that had already caused trouble, and copied it that evening.

grounding: A graduate links the instalment to auto-debit a day after salary credit and sets a balance alert, since automation prevents forgetting but the balance still needs watching.

subtype: Approach: inversion asking how the offer could be a trap [Thinking]
passage: The offer expired at midnight, or so the message said. Ten percent every month, the college senior had written, guaranteed, only for ten students. Vaibhav sat on the hostel stairs with a phone at ten percent battery and asked Reena what she would do. Instead of answering, Vaibhav started thinking aloud. "Suppose this is real. Then the person paying ten percent a month must earn more than that on the money every month, without fail, in a way that has no risk. Who can do that? If someone could, would they need my savings at all?" Reena stayed quiet. "And why the deadline?" Vaibhav muttered. "Real chances don't disappear at midnight." The message went unanswered, and the phone was put on charge.

qa.q: At what time did the offer say it would expire?
qa.a: The offer said it would expire at midnight.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav thinking about the guaranteed return?
qa.a: Vaibhav doubted it, wondering how anyone could earn more than ten percent a month without risk, and why they would need other people's savings.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav do next about the message, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could show it to a trusted adult or the bank's helpline and not reply, because offers like this are common warning signs.

qa.q: How might the college senior who sent the message see Vaibhav's questions?
qa.a: The sender may be pushing hard and may not like the questions, since a genuine offer would stand up to them.

grounding: A student offered a guaranteed monthly return asks what would have to be true for it to be real and sees that no lawful investment can promise it.

subtype: Approach: check registration with the regulator before paying [Action]
passage: Nour had saved for two years in a café job in Rotterdam, and a colleague's cousin recommended an online platform and an adviser with a slick brochure. Before sending anything, Nour sat with the laptop and Chen, a flatmate, at the kitchen table. "First step," Nour said, "find the public register of the national financial regulator." They typed the platform's name. No match. They typed the adviser's name. Nothing again. Chen searched for reviews and found a string of complaints about withdrawals not arriving. It took twelve minutes. "Convincing brochure, though," Chen said. Nour closed the laptop and said, "That was cheaper than finding out the hard way." The brochure went into the recycling.

qa.q: How long did the checking take?
qa.a: It took twelve minutes.

qa.q: What did Nour feel about closing the laptop and the brochure?
qa.a: Nour felt relieved at not having lost money, since the checking was cheaper than finding out the hard way.

qa.q: What could Nour do next if still wanting to invest, and why?
qa.a: Nour could talk to a licensed adviser found on the official register, because a registered person can be held to rules.

qa.q: How might Chen see Nour's plan to check before paying?
qa.a: Chen seems glad to help and impressed that a persuasive pitch did not win.

grounding: Before sending money a person checks whether the platform and adviser are on the regulator's register and reads complaints.

subtype: Approach: fear of missing out drives a quick decision [Pitfall]
passage: In the office pantry, Francis scrolled through a tip group where screenshots of gains kept arriving. Colleagues had said they were doubling money in a week. Someone posted "last chance today, closing in one hour". Francis felt the hurry rise in the chest, did not check who ran the group, and moved the whole month's savings to the account given. Ten minutes later the group went silent and the admin left. Sumit from accounts found Francis staring at the phone and said, "Show me." The screenshots were the same picture with different names. Sumit walked Francis to the desk phone and they called the bank's fraud line together, then filed the report on the official cybercrime portal. The money could not be recovered.

qa.q: How much time did the last chance message say was left?
qa.a: The message said the group was closing in one hour.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when moving the savings?
qa.a: Francis felt a rush of hurry and fear of missing out, and did not stop to check who ran the group.

qa.q: What could Francis do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Francis could pause for a day, ask who runs the group and talk to a trusted person, because urgency and social proof are used to stop checking.

qa.q: How might Sumit see the situation?
qa.a: Sumit likely feels concerned for Francis and acts quickly by phoning the bank's fraud line and helping to report it.

grounding: Seeing others post gains, a young worker rushes into a tip group and transfers savings within an hour, and the money cannot be recovered.

subtype: Approach: slow down and sleep on any pressured offer [Thinking]
passage: Lalremsiami, you asked how I stay away from those "invest now" messages. I keep one simple rule: nothing moves for forty-eight hours. Not a rupee. When a friend says only ten places are left, I say, "Thanks, I'll think and reply in two days." I used to feel a cold pull, like I would lose something. Now I know that pull is the pressure, not the proof. After a day or two, the urgency fades, and my head is clearer. A genuine chance will still be there on the third day. If it disappears, it wasn't a chance. So far, two offers vanished on their own and one I went on to look at properly. Waiting cost me nothing. It's the cheapest tool I own. Vishal

qa.q: For how long does nothing move under Vishal's rule?
qa.a: Nothing moves for forty-eight hours.

qa.q: How does Vishal feel about the pull of an urgent offer?
qa.a: Vishal used to feel a cold pull of fear at losing something, and now knows that the pull is pressure and not proof.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami do to try the rule, and why?
qa.a: Lalremsiami could tell the sender that a reply will come in two days, because time weakens pressure and leaves room to check.

qa.q: How might a friend who says only ten places are left see the reply?
qa.a: That friend might feel a little annoyed at first, but a genuine offer can still wait for a considered answer.

grounding: A person adopts a rule of waiting before any money moves for an investment, since time reduces the pull of urgency.

subtype: Approach: consult a trusted family member or a registered adviser [Action]
passage: At the bus stop in a small town in Bihar, Tushar showed a printed pamphlet to an uncle who worked in a bank. It promised a doubled sum in a year and had no company address. The uncle read it slowly and shook his head. "Where is the paperwork? Who is the seller? Who checks them?" On Saturday Tushar took the same pamphlet to Rukmini, a registered adviser with a small office near the market. Rukmini looked at it for a minute and said no genuine product doubles money that fast, and that a real firm would give papers and a registration number. Tushar walked out lighter. When the pamphlet-seller called that evening, Tushar said politely, "No, thank you. I have checked, and the answer is no."

qa.q: Who did Tushar show the pamphlet to first?
qa.a: Tushar showed the pamphlet first to an uncle who worked in a bank.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel when saying no to the seller?
qa.a: Tushar felt lighter and confident, since two people had pointed to the same problems.

qa.q: What could Tushar do if the seller keeps calling, and why?
qa.a: Tushar could stop answering and tell the uncle, because repeated pressure is a warning sign.

qa.q: How might the uncle see a young relative bringing the pamphlet?
qa.a: The uncle probably feels glad to be asked and worried about the pamphlet, and points out missing paperwork.

grounding: A student shows the offer to an uncle who works in a bank and to a registered adviser, and both point out unrealistic returns and no paperwork.

subtype: Approach: small test amount that grows into a big commitment [Pitfall]
passage:
Subject: I am sorry, Salma

Dear Salma,

I have to tell you what I did. Three months ago I put a small amount into an app, and within a week it paid a small profit. It felt like proof. So I put in a larger amount, then more, and I told you and two others to try it. Every time I wanted to stop, I thought: I have already put in so much, I cannot leave now. Yesterday I tried to withdraw and it asked for another fee. I now see that the first payout was the bait, and I brought you into it.

Please stop paying anything. Tomorrow I will go to the bank and report it, and I will tell my parents.

Ritu

qa.q: What happened when Ritu tried to withdraw yesterday?
qa.a: The app asked for another fee when Ritu tried to withdraw.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel each time Ritu wanted to stop paying?
qa.a: Ritu felt trapped, thinking so much had already been put in that leaving was impossible, so Ritu kept paying.

qa.q: What could Salma do after reading the email, and why?
qa.a: Salma could stop paying, keep the messages and tell a trusted adult, because more payments only add to the loss.

qa.q: How might Salma feel on learning that Ritu brought Salma in?
qa.a: Salma may feel worried and perhaps upset, but Ritu's honest warning gives a chance to stop before more is lost.

grounding: A first small payout from a fake app builds trust, so the person invests more and recruits others, and sunk cost keeps the paying going.

subtype: Approach: report and stop after noticing withdrawal blocks [Revision]
passage:
Arnab: the app wants another 5,000 fee to release my withdrawal
Sunaina: didn't you already pay a fee last week?
Arnab: yes. and one before. every time I pay, there's a new reason
Sunaina: that sounds like a pattern
Arnab: it is. I just saw it. I'm going to stop paying
Sunaina: what about the money already in?
Arnab: I can't get it back by paying more. I've saved every chat and screenshot
Sunaina: then what?
Arnab: tonight I'll call the bank and block the payments. tomorrow I'll report it on the official online cybercrime site
Sunaina: I'll come with you if you want
Arnab: yes please. I'd rather not do it alone

qa.q: How much was the new fee the app asked for?
qa.a: The app asked for another 5,000 fee to release the withdrawal.

qa.q: What did Arnab realise about the repeated fees?
qa.a: Arnab felt alarmed and then resolved, realising that each payment brought a new reason for another fee, which was a pattern, and decided to stop paying.

qa.q: What could Arnab do after filing the complaint, and why?
qa.a: Arnab could stay away from anyone who offers to recover the money for a fee, because that is often another trick.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see Arnab's decision to stop and report?
qa.a: Sunaina supports Arnab and offers to come along, which suggests concern and relief that the payments will stop.

grounding: When an app asks for a further fee to release money, a person sees the pattern, stops paying, saves chats and files complaints with the bank and cybercrime portal.
